power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is increasingly recognized as a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder in which motor-neuron degeneration is accompanied by widespread alterations in cortical dynamics.
Hyperexcitability is widespread across the brain, although more predominantly in motor and premotor areas.
Yet, how local excitability imbalance shapes distributed whole-brain dynamics remains poorly understood.

Here, we combined source-reconstructed resting-state magnetoencephalography data, tractography-informed whole-brain modeling, and simulation-based inference to investigate whether ALS-related alterations in large-scale brain dynamics can be mechanistically explained by changes in cortical excitability.
First, we characterized empirical brain dynamics using neuronal avalanche transition matrices (ATMs) on source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography data.
These analyses revealed significant alterations in ALS patients relative to healthy controls.
To interpret these changes mechanistically, we employed a reduced Wong-Wang whole-brain model in which local recurrent excitation modulates emergent large-scale neural dynamics.
The model showed that increasing recurrent excitation 1.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons, ultimately leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and death [1].
text.formatted: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons, ultimately leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and death <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Although its clinical manifestations are well described, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain only partially understood.
One of the most consistent neurophysiological findings in ALS is cortical hyperexcitability [2] [3] [4], with potential utility for prognosis and stratification [5].
text.formatted: One of the most consistent neurophysiological findings in ALS is cortical hyperexcitability <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, with potential utility for prognosis and stratification <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can be used to assess short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), which indexes cortical excitability, by probing GABA-A-mediated inhibitory interneuronal circuitry [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can be used to assess short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), which indexes cortical excitability, by probing GABA-A-mediated inhibitory interneuronal circuitry <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Reduced SICI reflects diminished inhibitory control and the consequent increase in neuronal recruitment.
SICI is diminished in ALS, both idiopathic and familial [9] [10] [11], before lower motor neuron impairment [2].
text.formatted: SICI is diminished in ALS, both idiopathic and familial <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, before lower motor neuron impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Increased cortical hyperexcitability has been linked to greater functional impairment, as measured by ALSFRS-R scores [12], while reduced average SICI independently predicts shorter survival in early-stage patients [13] [14] [15].
text.formatted: Increased cortical hyperexcitability has been linked to greater functional impairment, as measured by ALSFRS-R scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, while reduced average SICI independently predicts shorter survival in early-stage patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Although cortical hyperexcitability has been extensively investigated in motor circuits, ALS-related alterations also involve regions beyond the motor system [16] [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: Although cortical hyperexcitability has been extensively investigated in motor circuits, ALS-related alterations also involve regions beyond the motor system <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the reorganization of brain dynamics extends beyond motor areas, encompassing the entire brain [20], and is strongly associated with clinical impairment [20] and with disease staging [21].
text.formatted: Accordingly, the reorganization of brain dynamics extends beyond motor areas, encompassing the entire brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, and is strongly associated with clinical impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> and with disease staging <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: These observations motivate investigation of how local circuit alterations interact with distributed network organization to shape whole-brain dysfunction.
This points to widespread changes in meso-scale circuitry that reverberate across the whole brain.

Together, these observations support the hypothesis that whole brain dysfunction in ALS is best understood as the result of the interaction between local cortical hyperexcitability and the active, potentially compensatory or maladaptive, functional reorganization of distributed brain networks.
However, the link between local cortical hyperexcitability and distributed brain dysfunction remains difficult to establish from empirical measurements alone.

TMS-derived metrics provide a powerful and clinically relevant index of inhibitory dysfunction within motor cortical circuits, but they do not directly reveal how altered excitation-inhibition reshapes whole-brain dynamics.

Conversely, whole-brain electrophysiological or imaging markers can capture distributed reorganization, but they remain largely descriptive unless embedded within a framework that explicitly models the underlying biophysical mechanisms.
These limitations motivate the adoption of model-based approaches [22].
text.formatted: These limitations motivate the adoption of model-based approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: In fact, mechanistic wholebrain models allow us to move beyond purely correlational analyses by simulating how different, nondirectly observable neurodegenerative processes may give rise to measurable large-scale brain dynamics [23] [24] [25].
text.formatted: In fact, mechanistic wholebrain models allow us to move beyond purely correlational analyses by simulating how different, nondirectly observable neurodegenerative processes may give rise to measurable large-scale brain dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: By comparing these simulated dynamics, generated by "virtual brain twins" with data recorded from individual patients, one can estimate latent pathophysiological variables, thereby characterizing the pathophysiological processes underlying the observed brain activity.
We hypothesized that model inversion would identify a recurrent-excitation parameter associated with ALS-related alterations in resting-state brain dynamics.
We further hypothesize that the correlation between motor-frontal hyperexcitability and clinically relevant features would be more prominent than that with non-frontal regions.

In this study, we analyzed a cohort of 39 patients diagnosed with ALS and 39 controls, for whom clinical parameters, source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography, and magnetic resonance data were acquired, as in [20].
text.formatted: In this study, we analyzed a cohort of 39 patients diagnosed with ALS and 39 controls, for whom clinical parameters, source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography, and magnetic resonance data were acquired, as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: First, we assessed whether features extracted from resting-state brain activity could distinguish ALS patients from controls and whether these alterations were associated with clinical outcomes.
The characterization of clinical features was performed under the hypothesis that aperiodic bursts of activity (i.e., neuronal avalanches) would index pathophysiological processess [20, 26] .
text.formatted: The characterization of clinical features was performed under the hypothesis that aperiodic bursts of activity (i.e., neuronal avalanches) would index pathophysiological processess <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref> .

text.text: This empirical characterization provided the basis for subsequent computational modeling and model-inversion analyses.

To test whether the observed changes in local excitability could explain the observed shifts in large-scale brain dynamics, we used the reduced Wong-Wang model [27, 28], which describes the mean synaptic activity of interacting excitatory populations.
text.formatted: To test whether the observed changes in local excitability could explain the observed shifts in large-scale brain dynamics, we used the reduced Wong-Wang model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>, which describes the mean synaptic activity of interacting excitatory populations.

text.text: Whole-brain neural activity was simulated by coupling neural masses via structural connectomes derived from diffusionweighted tractography [29, 30].
text.formatted: Whole-brain neural activity was simulated by coupling neural masses via structural connectomes derived from diffusionweighted tractography <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: Because of its low-dimensional formulation, this model is particularly well-suited to whole-brain simulations aimed at linking regional excitability-related parameters to emergent macroscale neural dynamics.

Along these lines, rather than explicitly introducing a separate parameter for inhibition, we abstracted the local excitation-inhibition balance within each cortical region through the recurrent excitation parameter.
Two complementary model configurations were examined.

In the first, we assumed spatially uniform recurrent excitation, and jointly inferred the global recurrentexcitation parameter w and the global coupling parameter G. This configuration allowed us to test whether ALS-related alterations in whole-brain dynamics were compatible with an overall increase [31] in recurrent excitation while accounting for the contribution of interregional coupling.
text.formatted: In the first, we assumed spatially uniform recurrent excitation, and jointly inferred the global recurrentexcitation parameter w and the global coupling parameter G. This configuration allowed us to test whether ALS-related alterations in whole-brain dynamics were compatible with an overall increase <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> in recurrent excitation while accounting for the contribution of interregional coupling.

text.text: In the second model configuration, we divided the brain into two anatomically defined partitions: a motor-frontal partition, including frontal and motor cortical areas, and a complementary partition comprising the remaining regions.
The second model configuration was motivated by the heterogeneous anatomical distribution of ALS-related pathology.

Although ALS primarily affects the motor system, including the primary motor cortex and corticospinal pathways, premotor and frontal association regions are also fre-quently involved, with the latter particularly implicated in patients exhibiting cognitive and behavioral impairment [?, [32] [33] [34] [35].
text.formatted: Although ALS primarily affects the motor system, including the primary motor cortex and corticospinal pathways, premotor and frontal association regions are also fre-quently involved, with the latter particularly implicated in patients exhibiting cognitive and behavioral impairment [?, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, although alterations may extend throughout the brain, the clinical manifestations of ALS are generally dominated by motor and, to a variable extent, frontal-executive dysfunction [36] [37] [38].
text.formatted: Conversely, although alterations may extend throughout the brain, the clinical manifestations of ALS are generally dominated by motor and, to a variable extent, frontal-executive dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: Based on these observations, we introduced a parsimonious anatomical subdivision into a motor-frontal partition comprising 34 regions, including primary motor, premotor, and frontal association cortices, and a complementary non-frontal partition comprising the remaining 46 regions.
Importantly, this subdivision does not imply that regions outside the motor-frontal partition are unaffected, nor that all regions within it are equally involved.

Rather, it provides a simplified, biologically motivated framework to test whether ALS-related alterations in local recurrent excitation are more pronounced in anterior regions than in the rest of the cortex.
In particular, we hypothesized the motorfrontal regions to be more strongly hyperexcitable and proportional to individual clinical features.

To test this hypothesis, separate recurrent-excitation parameters, w F and w N F , were assigned to the two partitions and jointly inferred with the global coupling parameter G. This allowed us to investigate the spatial heterogeneity of inferred recurrent excitation while accounting for interregional coupling.
Both configurations were inferred independently using summary features extracted from whole-brain avalanche transition matrices.
To this end, we adopted a Bayesian framework based on simulation-based inference (SBI) [39], which enables efficient inversion of complex generative models [40, 41].
text.formatted: To this end, we adopted a Bayesian framework based on simulation-based inference (SBI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>, which enables efficient inversion of complex generative models <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>.

text.text: This approach was applied at the individual level, allowing us to investigate both group-level alterations and interindividual variability in inferred parameters.
Finally, we examined whether the estimated parameters were associated with clinical measures of functional impairment and disease staging.
An overview of the computational framework is provided in Fig. 1.
text.formatted: An overview of the computational framework is provided in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>.

text.text: In this study, we set out to identify informative features from MEG data acquired in ALS patients and controls (CTRL), and to produce a generative model to explain empirical data features as a function of local hyperexcitability.
We identified neuronal avalanches as bursts of activities spreading across the whole brain, using a threshold-based approach [42], and turned to avalanche-based metrics (see also Methods).
text.formatted: We identified neuronal avalanches as bursts of activities spreading across the whole brain, using a threshold-based approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>, and turned to avalanche-based metrics (see also Methods).

text.text: To characterize the spatial propagation of neuronal avalanches, we computed the Avalanche Transition Matrices (ATM) [43].
text.formatted: To characterize the spatial propagation of neuronal avalanches, we computed the Avalanche Transition Matrices (ATM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref>.

text.text: Each entry ATM ij encodes the probability that a suprathreshold activation in region i is followed by one in region j , within the same neuronal avalanche and then averaged across all avalanches.
These matrices therefore describe how transient regional activations propagate through the brain.
The ATM is intrinsically directed, as the probability that activation in region i is followed by activation in region j need not equal the probability of the reverse transition.
Fig. 2 displays the ATM averaged across ALS patients (Fig. 2a) and healthy controls (Fig. 2b).
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> displays the ATM averaged across ALS patients (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref>) and healthy controls (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2b</ref>).

text.text: Warmer colors correspond to higher transition probabilities between brain regions.
Fig. 2 (c-h) report the distributions of the selected metrics of interest (MOIs).
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2 (c-h</ref>) report the distributions of the selected metrics of interest (MOIs).

text.text: We computed the mean and median separately for the strictly upper and lower triangles, excluding the diagonal, and complemented these summaries with their Frobenius norm and entropy of the full matrix.
Under the regional ordering held constant across participants and simulations, the two triangles summarize opposite directions for the same unordered pairs of regions.
They provide complementary descriptions of the directed transition structure, rather than representing distinct anatomical subnetworks.
Here, directionality refers to the temporal ordering of activations and does not establish causal influence between regions.
The mean ATMs averages the transition probabilities across the regional pairs included in the analysis and therefore summarizes the overall propensity for activity propagation during avalanches.
Higher mean ATM values indicate that suprathreshold activation in one region is, on average, more likely to be followed by suprathreshold activation in another region.

ALS patients exhibited higher mean and median transition probabilities in the upper triangle than controls (Fig. 2c, mean: Cohen's d = 0.83, 95% CI [0.41, 1.29], p = 0.000523; panel e, median: d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.41, 1.32], p = 0.000480).
text.formatted: ALS patients exhibited higher mean and median transition probabilities in the upper triangle than controls (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2c</ref>, mean: Cohen's d = 0.83, 95% CI [0.41, 1.29], p = 0.000523; panel e, median: d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.41, 1.32], p = 0.000480).

text.text: In the lower triangle, the mean was also higher in ALS (Fig. 2d) (d = 0.47, 95% CI [0.03, 0.95], p = 0.0419), whereas the median (Fig. 2f) showed a smaller, nonsignificant difference in the same direction (d = 0.39, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.87], p = 0.0932).
text.formatted: In the lower triangle, the mean was also higher in ALS (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2d</ref>) (d = 0.47, 95% CI [0.03, 0.95], p = 0.0419), whereas the median (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2f</ref>) showed a smaller, nonsignificant difference in the same direction (d = 0.39, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.87], p = 0.0932).

text.text: Together, these findings indicate higher average avalanche transition probabilities in ALS, consistent with an enhanced propensity for large-scale activity propagation.
ATM entropy (Fig. 2g) showed a negative but nonsignificant group difference (d = -0.27, 95% CI [-0.73, 0.18], p = 0.238).
text.formatted: ATM entropy (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2g</ref>) showed a negative but nonsignificant group difference (d = -0.27, 95% CI [-0.73, 0.18], p = 0.238).

text.text: This measure quantifies the distribution of normalized singular values, with lower entropy indicating a greater concentration of spectral weight in fewer dominant components.
Higher entropy reflects a more even contribution of multiple spectral modes.
Stronger propagation does not necessarily imply greater spectral diversity, as transition probabilities may increase without substantially changing their relative spectral organization.
Although the negative effect estimate was consistent with a greater concentration of spectral weight in dominant modes, the group difference was not statistically significant.
Together, these findings indicate that group differences were more pronounced in the strength of avalanche propagation than in the spectral organization of the underlying transition matrix.
The Frobenius norm of the ATM (Fig. 2h) was higher in ALS patients (d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.12, 1.03], p = 0.0182) , indicating an increased overall magnitude of avalanche transition probabilities.
text.formatted: The Frobenius norm of the ATM (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2h</ref>) was higher in ALS patients (d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.12, 1.03], p = 0.0182) , indicating an increased overall magnitude of avalanche transition probabilities.

text.text: The convergent increases in mean, median, and norm support an amplification of avalanche-mediated activity spreading at the whole-brain level, compatible with the hypothesis of cortical hyperexcitability in ALS.
We additionally investigated whether the six empirical ATM features were associated with functional impairment and disease staging in ALS patients.
Spearman rank-order correlations were computed between each feature and ALSFRS-R, King's stage, and MiToS stage (Supplementary Fig. SM1).
text.formatted: Spearman rank-order correlations were computed between each feature and ALSFRS-R, King's stage, and MiToS stage (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">SM1</ref>).

text.text: Although some associations were observed, only the median of the upper-triangular entries was associated with King's stage at the nominal significance level (Spearman's ρ = 0.345, unadjusted p = 0.0425, q = 0.1102).
None of the associations survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the three clinical scales within each metric.

Thus, the empirical ATM features revealed alterations in large-scale brain dynamics at the group level but did not exhibit detectable corrected 5 . associations with the examined clinical outcomes when considered individually.

To mechanistically interpret the empirical alterations described above, we investigated whether the largescale dynamical signatures extracted from resting-state MEG recordings could emerge from changes in recurrent excitation and interregional coupling within a tractography-informed whole-brain model.
We employed a reduced Wong-Wang neural mass model in which regional excitatory populations interact through empirical structural connectivity (Fig. 3a; see Methods).
text.formatted: We employed a reduced Wong-Wang neural mass model in which regional excitatory populations interact through empirical structural connectivity (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3a</ref>; see Methods).

text.text: The parameter w controls recurrent excitation uniformly across regions, whereas the global coupling parameter G scales interactions between regions.
Representative simulated synaptic activity and empirical MEG signals are illustrated in Fig. 3b.
text.formatted: Representative simulated synaptic activity and empirical MEG signals are illustrated in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3b</ref>.

text.text: To examine the contributions of these two mechanisms, we varied w and G jointly over the ranges [2, 4] and [1.5, 2.5], respectively.
text.formatted: To examine the contributions of these two mechanisms, we varied w and G jointly over the ranges <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref> and [1.5, 2.5], respectively.

text.text: For each simulation, we computed the same six whole-brain ATM features used to characterize the empirical recordings: the mean and median of the upper and lower triangles, the Frobenius norm, and SVD-based entropy.
Each feature was independently normalized across the simulation ensemble.
The resulting parameter-space maps show how these observables depend on the combination of local recurrent excitation and global coupling (Fig. 3c-h).
text.formatted: The resulting parameter-space maps show how these observables depend on the combination of local recurrent excitation and global coupling (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3c-h</ref>).

text.text: Mean and median transition probabilities generally increased with w in both triangles of the ATM, accompanied by an increase in the Frobenius norm.
These changes indicate that stronger recurrent excitation enhances the propensity for avalanche-related activity to propagate across the network.
Global coupling also modulated these features: at a given excitation level, differences in G shifted the resulting transition statistics.
Thus, the magnitude of avalanche propagation reflected contributions from both local recurrent excitation and interactions mediated by structural connectivity.
ATM entropy showed an opposing overall pattern, with lower values at higher recurrent excitation.
Because this measure summarizes the distribution of normalized singular values, its reduction indicates that the transition matrix becomes more strongly dominated by a smaller number of components.
Stronger propagation can therefore coexist with a more concentrated organization of avalanche-related interactions, consistent with the reinforcement of dominant configurations.
The direction of the simulated increases in the ATM mean, median, and norm, along with the positive ALS -CTRL effect sizes observed empirically, are consistent with hyperexcitability in ALS patents.
The simulated decrease in entropy matched the direction of the (nonsignificant) empirical effect in the same direction.
The dependence of the features on both w and G means that the empirical alterations cannot be attributed to recurrent excitation from these qualitative comparisons alone.

We therefore used the simulated feature vectors to train a joint inference model for p(w, G | y), allowing us to estimate the recurrent excitation and the global coupling while also assessing the corresponding uncertainty.
Using simulations sampled from uniform priors over w ∈ [2, 4] and G ∈ [1.5, 2.5], we trained a neural density estimator to approximate the joint posterior p(w, G | y) (Fig. 4a).
text.formatted: Using simulations sampled from uniform priors over w ∈ <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref> and G ∈ [1.5, 2.5], we trained a neural density estimator to approximate the joint posterior p(w, G | y) (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4a</ref>).

text.text: This analysis tested whether the two parameters could be distinguished despite their overlapping effects on large-scale activity propagation.
Validation in 800 held-out synthetic simulations revealed different levels of recovery precision for the two parameters.

In this study, we combined source-reconstructed MEG recordings, whole-brain dynamical modeling, and simulation-based inference to investigate whether alterations in large-scale brain dynamics in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) could be explained by changes in recurrent excitation.

Building on previous analyses of this cohort [20] and established whole-brain modeling approaches [27, 28], we first characterized the empirical dynamics using directed avalanche transition matrices (ATMs).

text.text: We then examined how recurrent excitation and interregional coupling shaped the corresponding observables in a reduced Wong-Wang model.

Finally, we inferred subject-specific model parameters using two complementary configurations: a spatially uniform model and a regional model distinguishing motor-frontal from the remaining brain regions.

The motor-frontal partition allowed us to examine whether whole-brain avalanche dynamics were compatible with preferential recurrent excitation in motor and frontal systems, motivated by their involvement in ALS.
This partition is a hypothesis-driven simplification of the disease's heterogeneous anatomical distribution.
In particular, it does not explicitly separate frontotemporal systems associated with cognitive and behavioral manifestations, which may occur independently of memory impairment.

Alternative partitions distinguishing extended motor, frontotemporal, and remaining regions could provide a more differentiated account, but would require additional validation of parameter identifiability and more refined clinical stratification, especially in terms of assessments of extra-motor symptoms.

The results indicate that ALS-related changes in avalanche propagation are consistent with increased model-derived recurrent excitation, while the regional parameterization reveals an association between motor-frontal excitation and functional impairment.

Importantly, the ATM describes the temporal ordering of suprathreshold activations within avalanche events, rather than direct anatomical or causal interactions.

The different effect magnitudes observed in the upper and lower triangular summaries reflect properties of the directed transition structure under the chosen regional ordering and should not be interpreted as evidence for alterations in distinct anatomical pathways.
In contrast to the measures of transition magnitude, SVD-based ATM entropy showed a negative but nonsignificant group difference.

Although stronger propagation could coexist with a greater concentration of activity in dominant dynamical configurations, the present results do not establish a reduction in the diversity or complexity of brain dynamics in ALS.
ATM-derived spectral entropy should be distinguished from sequence-based measures of neural complexity, such as Lempel-Ziv complexity.

While the latter quantifies the diversity and compressibility of temporal or spatiotemporal activity sequences, ATM spectral entropy characterizes the distribution of singular-value weight in a matrix summarizing interregional avalanche propagation.
Accordingly, these measures capture different properties of neural dynamics and need not exhibit the same relationship with cortical excitability.
In fact, some models suggest that excitability would relate to higher complexity [46], while others point in the opposite direction.

Therefore, our findings do not establish a reduction in temporal neural complexity in ALS.
Overall, the most consistent empirical finding was an increase in avalanche-related transition strength.

The modeling results provide a mechanistic bridge between the empirical alterations observed in ALS and recurrent excitation, which is not directly observable from the MEG features, and is understood here as a hidden variable.
Hence, the model's epistemic scope accounts to providing a possible mechanistic interpretation of these observations.

Because the inferred parameters are estimated from the empirical observables, they cannot be interpreted as providing independent information absent from those inputs.
Their principal contribution lies instead in translating descriptive properties of large-scale activity into parameters with a defined role in a generative dynamical model.

Unlike the original ATM summaries, these parameters can be systematically varied to investigate the consequences of altered recurrent excitation and coupling, including dynamical regimes not directly sampled in the empirical recordings.

Such simulations provide a basis for formulating mechanistic hypotheses and potentially testable predictions, rather than establishing diagnostic or clinical predictive utility, which will require perspective validation.
We also evaluated the generative model against empirical observations by producing subject-specific simulations using the inferred posterior mean parameters.
For each participant, ten stochastic realizations were generated and the resulting ATM features were compared with those extracted from MEG recordings (Fig. 9).

text.text: These analyses assessed whether the inferred parameter configurations could generate dynamical summaries compatible with the observations and characterized variability across noise realizations.
The distribution of the empirical and simulated features were overlapping.
However, one should keep in mind that the inference had been performed utilizing normalized data and, as such, the simulations also underent the respective anti-transformation.
Hence, the similarity of the distributions should not be interpreted in terms of raw , but rather relative, magnitudes.
These analyses therefore constitute a model-fit assessment rather than complete posterior predictive validation.
A complementary test of the simulated dynamics was obtained by examining neuronal avalanche-size and duration distributions (Supplementary Figs. SM6-SM9).
text.formatted: A complementary test of the simulated dynamics was obtained by examining neuronal avalanche-size and duration distributions (Supplementary Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">SM6-SM9</ref>).

text.text: Both empirical recordings and subject-specific simulations exhibited broad, decreasing distributions, indicating qualitative similarities in avalanche-like activity.

The estimated avalanche-size exponents showed no statistically detectable difference between empirical and simulated data in controls after multiple-comparison correction, whereas simulated exponents were significantly higher in ALS patients.
For avalanche durations, simulated exponents were systematically lower than their empirical counterparts in both groups.

These discrepancies are informative because the inference procedure was constrained by ATM-derived features describing sequential regional recruitment within avalanches, whereas the distributions of avalanche size and duration were not directly fitted.

Although avalanche duration may indirectly influence the number of transitions contributing to an ATM, neither the total amplitude-weighted avalanche size nor the full distribution of event durations are explicitly encoded by the selected summary statistics.
The differences mentioned above identify aspects of the empirical dynamics that the present model does not fully capture and may provide useful additional constraints for future model development.
Furthermore, approximate scaling over a restricted range should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of criticality or of a unique power-law generating mechanism.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the reduced Wong-Wang model represents recurrent excitation without explicitly resolving inhibitory populations.

The inferred parameters may therefore reflect effective changes in the excitation-inhibition balance, but the model cannot distinguish altered excitatory feedback from changes in inhibitory regulation.
Second, all participants were simulated using a common structural connectome [43] derived from healthy subjects, rather than individual connectomes.
text.formatted: Second, all participants were simulated using a common structural connectome <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> derived from healthy subjects, rather than individual connectomes.

text.text: Because recurrent excitation, global coupling, and network topology jointly influence whole-brain dynamics, the inferred parameters may partially accommodate effects of unmodeled individual or disease-related structural differences.
Estimating global coupling as a free parameter does not eliminate this limitation, since a scalar parameter cannot reproduce changes in connection topology.
Finally, independent physiological measures of cortical excitability, such as TMSderived indices, were unavailable for this cohort.
Future studies should assess sensitivity to alternative connectomes and incorporate patient-specific structural connectivity where feasible.
Overall, the present study links alterations in large-scale avalanche propagation in ALS to changes in the recurrent-excitation parameters of a whole-brain generative model.

The results support a distributed increase in model-derived recurrent excitation, with a larger observed motor-frontal group effect and an association between motor-frontal excitation and functional impairment.

Beyond the discrimination of patients from controls, the main value of the framework is its capacity to provide a mechanistically interpretable representation of empirical dynamics and to generate model-dependent predictions that can be tested in future physiological and longitudinal studies.

This common anatomical scaffold was employed in both the spatially uniform and regional model configurations, ensuring that differences in simulated dynamics arose from variations in the model parameters rather than from differences in the underlying structural network.

We characterized whole-brain dynamics using six summary features derived from directed Avalanche Transition Matrices (ATMs): the mean and median of the strictly upper and lower triangles, the Frobenius norm, and singular-value-based entropy.
The same feature definitions and regional ordering were used for empirical recordings and simulated activity.
Starting from source-reconstructed MEG signals, each regional time series is first standardized using a z-score transformation.
To determine the activation threshold, we examined the distribution of standardized activity across participants and identified the point at which it deviated from a Gaussian distribution [42].
text.formatted: To determine the activation threshold, we examined the distribution of standardized activity across participants and identified the point at which it deviated from a Gaussian distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: This deviation occurred at approximately 2.5 standard deviations, which was therefore adopted as the threshold for identifying suprathreshold activity.
Time points exceeding this threshold are considered active, resulting in a binarized representation of the data.
Based on this representation, neuronal avalanches are defined as contiguous periods of activity bounded by time bins in which no regions are active.
The size of an avalanche is defined as the cumulative suprathreshold amplitude excess of the z-scored regional signals, summed over all regions and time samples belonging to each avalanche.
Specifically, for an activation threshold of (|σ| = 2.5), avalanche size was calculated as ∑︁ r,t∈A max(|z r (t)|-2.5, 0).
Avalanche duration corresponds to the number of consecutive time bins during which the avalanche persists.
To validate the presence of neuronal avalanches, we examine the distributions of avalanche sizes and durations, which are reported in the Supplementary Material.
These distributions exhibit power-law behavior, consistent with the characteristic signatures of avalanche dynamics in neural systems [54, 55].
text.formatted: These distributions exhibit power-law behavior, consistent with the characteristic signatures of avalanche dynamics in neural systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55]</ref>.

text.text: Within each detected avalanche, we analyze the spatiotemporal propagation of activity by constructing avalanche transition matrices (ATMs) [20].

text.text: Each ATM encodes the probability that activation in one region is followed by activation in another region in the subsequent time step.
Avalanches shorter than two samples were excluded.
Avalanche-specific transition estimates were aggregated into a subject-level Avalanche Transition Matrix (ATM).
The matrices were retained in their directed, non-symmetrized form, preserving differences between opposite transition directions.
Accordingly, ATM ij and ATM ji were not constrained to be equal.
Directionality denotes temporal ordering of suprathreshold activations and does not establish causal influence.

Subsequently, data features are extracted from the avalanche transition matrices (ATMs), including the mean value, median for the upper and lower triangles to take into account the directionality of the transitions, Frobenius norm and entropy.
For each participant, the mean ATM was calculated as the arithmetic mean of the entries included in the analyses.
It summarizes the average transition probability across regional pairs and therefore characterizes the average propensity for avalanche-related activity propagation.
The Frobenius norm was calculated as the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries and quantifies the overall magnitude of the transition weights.
Unlike the mean, it gives greater weight to larger entries.
To characterize the organization of the directed matrix, we computed Shannon entropy from its normalized singular values.

For the model inversion procedure, all selected metrics were subsequently normalized to the [0,1] range using min-max scaling.

This was done to place heterogeneous features on a common scale and to ensure that the inference procedure focused on reproducing the relative pattern of alterations observed across empirical metrics, rather than the absolute values of the individual metrics.
Accordingly, the objective of the inversion was not to match the exact magnitude of each individual metric, but to capture the overall trend and relationships characterizing the empirical data.

The Bayesian framework provides a principled approach for parameter estimation, prediction, and uncertainty quantification by updating prior knowledge with evidence from empirical observations [56].
text.formatted: The Bayesian framework provides a principled approach for parameter estimation, prediction, and uncertainty quantification by updating prior knowledge with evidence from empirical observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: In this setting, uncertainty is explicitly represented through probability distributions: prior beliefs about model parameters are updated using observed data to obtain posterior distributions.

However, performing Bayesian inference on large-scale brain data is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the observations, the nonlinearity of brain dynamics, and the complex interactions imposed by the underlying brain network structure.
In particular, the likelihood function is typically computationally intractable for such models, making conventional approaches such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) computationally expensive [39].
text.formatted: In particular, the likelihood function is typically computationally intractable for such models, making conventional approaches such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) computationally expensive <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: To overcome these limitations, we adopt a likelihood-free approach based on Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) [57, 58], in which the computational model is treated as a stochastic simulator capable of generating synthetic data that resemble empirical observations.
text.formatted: To overcome these limitations, we adopt a likelihood-free approach based on Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58]</ref>, in which the computational model is treated as a stochastic simulator capable of generating synthetic data that resemble empirical observations.

text.text: This framework enables parameter inference without explicitly evaluating the likelihood function.

Specifically, we use neural density estimation techniques based on Normalizing Flows (NFs), which learn flexible transformations from simple base distributions (e.g., the prior) to complex posterior distributions.
By construction, these transformations are invertible and differentiable, enabling efficient sampling and exact likelihood or density evaluation.
Our objective is to infer the posterior distribution of the model excitability parameters that best explain the observed empirical features.
To this end, we considered two complementary model configurations.
In the first spatially uniform configuration, a single global excitability parameter (w) controlled the excitability of all brain regions, while G scaled interregional coupling.
Joint inference of (w, G) addressed whether the empirical dynamics were compatible with increased recurrent excitation when global coupling was also allowed to vary.
This configuration therefore provided a parsimonious assessment of a spatially uniform alteration in excitation without fixing the coupling regime.
In the partition-specific configuration, the uniform excitation parameter was replaced by w F for the 34 motor-frontal regions and w NF for the remaining 46 regions.
Global coupling G remained an inferred parameter.
Joint inference of (w F , w NF , G) allowed us to examine whether the empirical dynamics were compatible with different excitation levels across the two anatomical partitions.
The uniform model is recovered when w F = w NF .
The two configurations thus address complementary questions concerning the overall elevation and regional distribution of recurrent excitation.
They were fitted separately; estimates from the uniform configuration were not used to fix G in the partition-specific inference.
Independent uniform priors were assigned to the parameters.
Recurrent-excitation parameters were sampled over [2, 4], and global coupling over [1.5, 2.5]: p regional (w F , w NF , G) = U(w F ; 2, 4) U(w NF ; 2, 4) U(G; 1.5, 2.5).

We employ Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (SNPE) [58], a simulation-based inference (SBI) framework that learns the relationship between model parameters and observed summary statistics directly from simulations.
text.formatted: We employ Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (SNPE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref>, a simulation-based inference (SBI) framework that learns the relationship between model parameters and observed summary statistics directly from simulations.

text.text: This approach is particularly well-suited for mechanistic whole-brain models, for which the likelihood functions are generally intractable.

The posterior density is approximated using a Masked Autoregressive Flow (MAF) [59], a class of normalizing flows that enables flexible and computationally efficient posterior density estimation through a sequence of invertible nonlinear transformations.
text.formatted: The posterior density is approximated using a Masked Autoregressive Flow (MAF) <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref>, a class of normalizing flows that enables flexible and computationally efficient posterior density estimation through a sequence of invertible nonlinear transformations.

text.text: SNPE requires three key components: (i) a prior distribution over parameters, (ii) a generative model capable of simulating brain activity for a given parameter configuration, and (iii) a set of lowdimensional features summarizing the empirical data.
In our case, the generative model is the reduced Wong-Wang whole-brain neural mass model, and the features are computed from source-reconstructed signals.
Specifically, we extract a set of summary statistics, as described in the previous paragraph.

For participant s, the trained estimators were conditioned on the empirical feature vector y s,expt to approximate for the uniform model configuration, and for the partition-specific model configuration.
Both configurations used the same six whole-brain ATM features computed on the whole brain.
Regional excitation parameters were therefore inferred from their combined effects on whole-brain dynamics, rather than from features computed separately within each anatomical partition.
Joint posterior sampling retained dependencies among excitation and coupling parameters, including potential compensatory relationships.
We generated 4,000 simulations for the spatially uniform configuration, jointly inferring (w, G), and 20,000 simulations for the partition-specific configuration, jointly inferring (w F , w NF , G).
The parameter vectors were sampled from the corresponding prior distributions.
Held-out simulations used for synthetic validation were excluded from training.
Once trained, each conditional density estimator was applied to participants' empirical feature vectors to evaluate and sample from the approximate posterior without additional simulations.
This amortized inference procedure does not require the generative model to be differentiable.
Before applying empirical observations, we evaluated parameter recovery using held-out synthetic simulations with known ground-truth parameters.
Test simulations were excluded from network training and generated using the same structural-connectivity matrix and simulation protocol as the training data.
The uniform-model ensemble comprised 4,000 simulations, of which 3,200 were assigned to training and 800 to held-out testing.
The regional-model ensemble comprised 20,000 simulations, partitioned into 16,000 training and 4,000 test simulations.
For each test simulation, the trained estimator was conditioned on the corresponding feature vector, and joint posterior samples were drawn.
Parameter recovery was evaluated by comparing posterior means with ground-truth values.
Marginal posterior uncertainty was summarized using posterior standard deviations and equal-tailed 95% credible intervals.

The quality of the inferred posteriors is assessed using diagnostic measures including posterior shrinkage and z-scores, defined as z = ( θ -θ true )/σ posterior , where θ is the posterior mean, θ true is the ground-truth parameter, and σ posterior is the posterior standard deviation.
We additionally evaluated marginal empirical coverage as the proportion of test simulations for which the 95% credible interval contained the ground-truth parameter.
Coverage was compared with the nominal 95% level, and recovery plots were examined across the parameter range to identify regions with larger errors.
High shrinkage was interpreted as posterior concentration rather than evidence of accurate recovery or calibration.
The illustrated posterior examples complement the evaluation across the full held-out set.
The resulting estimates exhibit low z-scores and high shrinkage, indicating accurate and informative Bayesian inference across the explored parameter range.

Reproduction of empirical features from inferred parameters.
For each of the 73 non-outlier subjects (38 ALS and 35 controls), the posterior means of w F , w N F , and G were used to generate ten stochastic simulations.
The parameter triplet was held fixed across simulations, while the random seed was varied to obtain distinct noise realizations.

Comparisons
We evaluated whether the inferred parameters discriminated ALS patients from healthy controls using separate classification models for each parameter.
Each participant contributed one observation, represented by the corresponding posterior mean; posterior samples were not treated as independent observations.
ALS was designated as the positive class.
Classification was performed using L2-regularized logistic regression and nested stratified five-fold cross-validation, repeated five times with different random partitions.
Identical outer splits were used across parameter-based classifiers.

Within each outer training set, the inverse regularization strength was selected from C ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100} using an inner stratified three-fold cross-validation, maximizing the mean validation ROC AUC.
Predictors were standardized using statistics estimated exclusively from the corresponding training folds.
For each repetition, predicted probabilities for the held-out participants were pooled across the five outer folds, yielding one out-of-fold prediction per par-ticipant.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed by varying the classification threshold and plotting sensitivity against the false-positive rate.
Discrimination was quantified by the area under the ROC curve (AUC).
We report the mean and standard deviation of the five repetitionspecific AUCs.
For visualization, ROC curves were interpolated onto a common false-positive-rate grid and averaged across repetitions.
This analysis assessed discrimination conditional on the previously estimated model parameters and the upstream preprocessing and subject-selection procedures.

The inference pipeline was not re-estimated within each classification fold; the evaluation therefore concerns the downstream classifier rather than an independently validated end-to-end diagnostic pipeline.

Figure1: Overview of the computational framework for estimating latent cortical excitability in ALS.

Synthetic signals were processed to extract the corresponding data features, which were used to train neural density estimators and approximate the posterior distributions of the model parameters conditioned on the empirical observations.
Model inversion and physiological interpretation.
